extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, scientists, and educated readers evaluating evolutionary explanations (readers of Origin of Species)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging whether particular instincts or behavioral traits can be explained by natural selection, including what counts as instinct, what evidence is needed (variation, inheritance, gradations), and how to use domestication and comparative observation as tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/identification of instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: An action, which we ourselves should require experience to enable us to perform, when performed by an animal, more especially by a very young one, without any experience, and when performed by many individuals in the same way, without their knowing for what purpose it is performed, is usually said to be instinctive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use criteria of (a) performance without prior experience, (b) occurrence in very young individuals, (c) conformity of action across many individuals, and (d) lack of apparent understanding of purpose. Examples: cuckoo laying eggs in other nests; aphides excreting for ants on antennal stimulation; young pointers pointing without training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex instincts require gradual accumulation of slight profitable variations
rubrics_metrics.description: No complex instinct can possibly be produced through natural selection, except by the slow and gradual accumulation of numerous, slight, yet profitable, variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To accept a natural-selection explanation for a complex instinct, seek evidence that many small advantageous changes, each beneficial to the individual, could have been accumulated. Examples and comparative gradations (ants, hive-bee, cuckoo) should be shown or argued to be possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of intermediate or collateral gradations
rubrics_metrics.description: We ought to find in nature, not the actual transitional gradations by which each complex instinct has been acquired—for these could be found only in the lineal ancestors of each species—but we ought to find in the collateral lines of descent some evidence of such gradations; or we ought at least to be able to show that gradations of some kind are possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct lineal intermediates are unavailable, look for related species or collateral lines showing partial or intermediate behaviours, or for homologies and possible transitional states (e.g., swim-bladder to lung). Absence of known intermediates should not be taken as decisive against gradual evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation and inheritance of instincts are necessary conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: As some degree of variation in instincts under a state of nature, and the inheritance of such variations, are indispensable for the action of natural selection ... instincts certainly do vary—for instance, the migratory instinct, both in extent and direction, and in its total loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require documented cases of behavioural variation and evidence (or plausible mechanism) of heritability. Use examples like differences in nests, migratory changes, fear responses, and domestic examples to establish that instincts vary and can be inherited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish habit-inheritance from selection of accidental variations
rubrics_metrics.description: If we suppose any habitual action to become inherited—and I think it can be shown that this does sometimes happen—then the resemblance between what originally was a habit and an instinct becomes so close as not to be distinguished. ... But it would be the most serious error to suppose that the greater number of instincts have been acquired by habit in one generation, and then transmitted by inheritance to succeeding generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a behaviour could plausibly have been fixed by long-continued habitual practice alone, or whether selection of minor accidental variations is a better explanation. Use domestication cases (pointers, tumblers) to separate the roles of habit and selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use domestication as experimental evidence for inherited behavioural variation
rubrics_metrics.description: The possibility, or even probability, of inherited variations of instinct in a state of nature will be strengthened by briefly considering a few cases under domestication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat changes under domestication (dogs pointing/retrievers, tumbler pigeons, loss of broodiness in fowls, tameness in dogs) as empirical tests: if selection or habit alters instincts in domestic breeds, analogous processes may operate in nature. Provide concrete breeding/observation evidence where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occasional advantageous habit can be fixed if heritable and beneficial
rubrics_metrics.description: If the old bird profited by this occasional habit, or if the young were made more vigorous by advantage having been taken of the mistaken maternal instinct of another bird ... then the old birds or the fostered young would gain an advantage ... By a continued process of this nature, I believe that the strange instinct of our cuckoo could be, and has been, generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing novel instincts (e.g., brood-parasitism), consider whether a once-occurring or occasional habit could confer a fitness advantage and be subject to inheritance and selection. Look for analogous occasional behaviours in related taxa as plausible starting points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinctive actions often resemble habits in performance but differ in origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Frederick Cuvier and several of the older metaphysicians have compared instinct with habit. This comparison gives ... an accurate notion of the frame of mind under which an instinctive action is performed, but not of its origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodologically, compare the behavioural form (sequence, rhythm, resistance to interruption) to habitual actions to diagnose instinctive structure, while separately investigating origin (habitual training vs inherited variation). Use experimental interruption examples (caterpillar hammock stages) to probe the sequence-character of instinctive acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural selection acts for the good of each species (not exclusively for others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural selection cannot possibly produce any modification in any one species exclusively for the good of another species. ... Natural selection acts solely by and for the good of each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject explanations that posit structures produced solely to benefit other species. Accept adaptations that are at least indirectly advantageous to the bearer even if they affect other species (e.g., excretions useful to ants but also convenient to aphides). Use counterexamples (rattle-as-warning myth) to illustrate invalid teleological reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptations must be on balance advantageous to the possessor
rubrics_metrics.description: No organ will be formed, as Paley has remarked, for the purpose of causing pain or for doing an injury to its possessor. If a fair balance be struck between the good and evil caused by each part, each will be found on the whole advantageous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess net fitness effects: even if a structure sometimes injures the individual (bee sting causing death), if overall it contributes to the species' or individual's reproductive success sufficiently, natural selection can explain its persistence. If net effect is harmful, expect modification or extinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection produces relative, not absolute, perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural selection tends only to make each organic being as perfect as, or slightly more perfect than, the other inhabitants of the same country with which it has to struggle for existence. ... Natural selection will not produce absolute perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate traits relative to local ecological competitors and conditions rather than against an ideal of absolute perfection. Use biogeographic comparisons (endemic New Zealand species vs introduced European species) and known imperfect organs (eye correction, sting withdrawal problem) as norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homologies and multifunctional intermediates facilitate transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The homologies of many organs and their intermediate states show that wonderful metamorphoses in function are at least possible. For instance, a swim-bladder has apparently been converted into an air-breathing lung. The same organ having performed simultaneously very different functions, and then having been specialised for one function ... must often have largely facilitated transitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing an evolutionary pathway for an instinct or organ, favour mechanisms involving pre-existing structures or behaviours that performed related functions (exaptation) and look for homologies that make functional shifts plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for life-stage, seasonal, or contextual variation as facilitators
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes of instinct may sometimes be facilitated by the same species having different instincts at different periods of life, or at different seasons of the year, or when placed under different circumstances ... in which case either one or the other instinct might be preserved by natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether multiple distinct behaviours occur across life stages or seasons; such within-species diversity can provide raw material for selection to favour one behaviour in new contexts. Cite examples where juvenile and adult instincts differ or seasonal behaviour shifts occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical observational and experimental support required
rubrics_metrics.description: I will select ... the cuckoo ... the slave-making instinct of certain ants; and the comb-making power of the hive-bee: these ... have generally been ranked by naturalists as the most wonderful of all known instincts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantiate claims about origins of instincts with careful field observations and, if possible, experiments (e.g., removing ants from aphides, opening nests of slave-making ants, breeding/domestication records). Use detailed case studies to test hypotheses about gradualness, utility, heredity, and mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautious epistemic stance in absence of full knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: We are far too ignorant, in almost every case, to be enabled to assert that any part or organ is so unimportant for the welfare of a species, that modifications in its structure could not have been slowly accumulated by means of natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid definitive negative conclusions based on current lack of information. Maintain caution about declaring traits inexplicable by selection; prioritize searching for evidence of variation, utility, homology, or collateral gradations before rejecting evolutionary explanations.
